purpose: User-directed investigation: DecodeBenchmarks/EncodeBenchmarks/ProgressiveDecodeBenchmarks (the only existing native-vs-managed comparison) measure exactly one image per [Benchmark] invocation, while the real usage pattern is loading a grid/session of 5-50+ thumbnails at once - the managed-only PictTag.PgfCodec.Performance.SessionWorkloadBenchmarks already models that batched shape, but its own doc comment explicitly defers 'the native comparison matrix' to PictTag.PgfCodec.Benchmarks, which never actually added one. Added BatchDecodeBenchmarks/BatchEncodeBenchmarks (new files in PictTag.PgfCodec.Benchmarks) - [Params(1, 10, 50)] batches of the same 20-dimension mixed-size/quality/pattern set SessionWorkloadBenchmarks uses (factored into a new shared BatchFixtures.cs so both native and managed legs decode/encode the identical fixture set), comparing NativeDecodeBatch/NativeEncodeBatch (baseline) against ManagedDecodeBatch/ManagedEncodeBatch (convenience API) and ManagedReusableDecodeBatch/ManagedWorkspaceEncodeBatch (the reusable-session/workspace contract a real batch-processing service would actually use).
methodology: BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun (IterationCount=3, WarmupCount=3), same job kind as the existing authoritative single-image comparison (2026-08-05-6f120cf-simd-scalar-controlled-shortrun) so the two are comparable. A preliminary Dry/ColdStart smoke test (not archived) showed a much more dramatic ratio - roughly 9-11x at BatchSize=1 narrowing to roughly 2-3x at BatchSize=50 - but that shape is a ColdStart/single-iteration artifact (JIT tiering promotion happening mid-measurement) specific to the Dry job, not evidence about steady-state throughput; this archived ShortRun result is the properly warmed-up measurement and shows a real but much smaller effect.
result: CONFIRMED, moderate real effect - not the dramatic gap the Dry smoke test suggested, but a genuine, consistent narrowing as batch size grows. Decode (AMD Ryzen 7 5800X): convenience ManagedDecodeBatch is 1.44x native at BatchSize=1, 1.47x at BatchSize=10, 1.22x at BatchSize=50; the reusable/workspace path (ManagedReusableDecodeBatch) is 1.28x/1.33x/1.19x across the same batch sizes and allocates roughly 250x less than the convenience path at every batch size (5,368 B vs 1,449,890 B at BatchSize=1; 333,216 B vs 141,893,994 B at BatchSize=50). Encode: ManagedEncodeBatch is 1.51x/1.23x/1.23x native; ManagedWorkspaceEncodeBatch is 1.56x/1.29x/1.08x - the workspace path shows the largest narrowing of any leg, nearly closing the gap with native entirely at BatchSize=50. Interpretation: the existing single-image DecodeBenchmarks/EncodeBenchmarks numbers are directionally correct (managed IS slower, by roughly this same order of magnitude) but modestly overstate the real-world gap for a realistic multi-image session, and materially understate how close the reusable/workspace paths get to native at real batch scale - the single-image comparison never exercises those paths' batch-amortized allocation savings the way SessionWorkloadBenchmarks' managed-only harness already does. See docs/benchmarks/pgfcodec/README.md's 'Native vs. managed' table for the interpreted numbers and the P/Invoke-interop fairness caveat (native here is measured via a P/Invoke transition, which a real standalone C++ application would not pay).
